title: Averaging many noisy trees
objectives: Reduce variance by averaging trees fitted to bootstrap samples.
Explain why bagging helps deep trees, not stumps, and why more trees never overfit.

explain.text: The error drops from 0.2965 at $B = 1$ to 0.2290 at $B = 20$, then only to 0.2075 by $B = 100$. This is **bagging**, short for bootstrap aggregating: resample the rows, grow a tree on each resample, and aggregate their votes.

screens.title: Why about 63%
screens.prose: Here 6 of the 10 loans appeared. For large books the share settles near 63%. Build the argument for one row, say loan 0, in a book of $n$ loans.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: One draw misses loan 0 with probability $1 - \frac{1}{n}$, since each of the $n$ loans is equally likely
The $n$ draws are independent, so all of them miss it with probability $\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^n$
As $n$ grows, $\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^n \to e^{-1} \approx 0.368$, the limit that defines $e$
So loan 0 appears at least once with probability $1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632$, the complement

hints.text: Start with a single draw.
Independence lets you multiply the miss chances of the $n$ draws.
One draw, then all $n$ draws, then the limit, then the complement.

feedback.correct: Every row has the same chance, so about 63% of rows appear in each resample.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Go from one draw, to all draws, to large $n$, to the complement.

byKey.comp: The complement needs the miss chance for large $n$ first.
byKey.lim: The limit is of the expression for all $n$ draws, so that line comes first.

explain.text: For $n = 10$ the miss chance is $0.9^{10} = 0.349$; for $n = 400$ it is $0.367$, already close to $e^{-1} = 0.368$. So about 63.2% of rows appear and 36.8% sit out of each resample.

screens.title: Why averaging works
screens.prose: Each tree's prediction for a loan is a random variable: it depends on the resample. If $B$ trees were independent, each with variance $\sigma^2$, then as in *Averages settle down* $$\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} \hat f_b(x)\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{B}.$$ Averaging leaves each tree's bias unchanged.
screens.question: One tree's $P(\text{default})$ for loan Q has sd 0.30 across resamples. What would the sd of the average of 9 independent trees be?

hints.text: The formula is for the variance. Square the sd first.
$\sigma^2 = 0.09$, so the variance of the average is $0.09/9$.

feedback.correct: Variance falls as $1/B$, so the sd falls as $1/\sqrt{B}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the variance by 9, then take the square root.

byKey.overB: You divided the sd by 9. The variance falls by 9, so the sd falls by $\sqrt{9} = 3$.
byKey.var: 0.01 is the variance of the average. Take its square root for the sd.
byKey.same: Averaging independent trees does shrink the spread. Divide the variance by 9.

explain.text: $0.30/\sqrt{9} = 0.10$. Our trees are not independent: any two share most of their rows and both split on leverage first. So their errors are correlated, and the variance stops falling long before $1/B$ would; lesson 6 measures by how much.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

NAMES = ["leverage", "cover", "margin", "vol", "short", "drawdown", "size", "age"]

def make_loans(seed, n=400):
    """n company loans, 8 features as z-scores across the book.
    y = 1 if the loan defaulted within a year. Leverage matters most;
    the next five matter a little; size and age carry no signal."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, 8))
    z = (-0.3 + 2.5 * X[:, 0]
         + 0.7 * (-X[:, 1] - X[:, 2] + X[:, 3] + X[:, 4] + X[:, 5]))
    y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
    return X, y

widget.solution:
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

def bagging_test_acc(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, n_estimators):
    accs = []
    for B in n_estimators:
        model = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=B,
                                  random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
        accs.append(round(float(model.score(X_test, y_test)), 4))
    return accs

screens.title: Fifty analysts
screens.prose: Fifty analysts forecast a company's annual earnings growth. Over many years, one analyst's error has sd 4.0%. The consensus, their plain average, has error sd 2.9%. With independent errors it would be $4.0/\sqrt{50} = 0.57\%$.
screens.question: Why does the consensus improve so much less than $1/\sqrt{50}$ promises?

options.text: Their errors are correlated: they read the same filings and hear the same guidance
Fifty forecasts are too few for averaging to work
options.why: You blamed the count. Fifty independent errors would give 0.57%; the shortfall comes from errors they share.

options.text: Averaging removes bias but cannot touch variance
options.why: That is the wrong way round. Averaging cuts variance and leaves bias alone.

options.text: Averaging only helps votes, not forecasts of numbers
options.why: Averaging works for numbers too: regression trees are bagged by averaging their predictions.

hints.text: When would 50 forecasts be no better than one?
If all 50 made the same mistake, averaging would change nothing.
Shared information makes the errors move together, so they do not cancel.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the analysts have in common.

byKey.few: Fifty is plenty when errors are independent. These are not.

explain.text: Errors that move together do not cancel in an average. Bagged trees have the same problem: they share most rows and the same strong feature. Lesson 6 gives the formula and a way to break the link.

ideas: A deep tree is a high-variance predictor: a resample of the same rows can move its splits and flip its answers.
Bagging grows a tree on each bootstrap sample and averages their probabilities, or votes; each sample holds about 63.2% of the rows, $1 - e^{-1}$.
Averaging cuts variance and leaves bias alone, so bag deep trees, not stumps; more trees never overfit, they just stop helping.

formula.name: Variance of an average of independent predictors
formula.note: Bagged trees are correlated, so the real variance falls more slowly.

summary.trap: A small dip in test error at some $B$ is noise. Extra trees cannot overfit; choose $B$ where the curve is flat.

quiz.prose: You fit one deep tree on all 400 loans. Then you put 50 copies of that same tree into a vote.
quiz.question: How does the vote's test error compare with the single tree's?

options.text: It is exactly the same
Lower, because 50 votes average out the noise
options.why: You expected any average to help. Fifty identical trees make identical mistakes, so nothing cancels.

options.text: Lower by a factor of $\sqrt{50}$
options.why: That needs independent errors. Copies are perfectly correlated.

options.text: Higher, because 50 trees overfit
options.why: Copying a tree changes nothing; the vote is the tree.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the 50 trees ever disagree.

explain.text: Every copy votes the same way on every loan, so the vote is the tree. Bagging gains only because bootstrap trees differ.

quiz.question: Which one gains most from bagging?

options.text: A deep, unpruned regression tree
A stump with one split
options.why: A stump hardly changes between resamples, so there is little variance to average away.

options.text: A linear regression on three features
options.why: OLS on a few features is already stable; its resampled fits barely differ.

options.text: A tree pruned to depth 2
options.why: Pruning has already cut most of the variance bagging would remove.

feedback.correct: Bagging cuts variance, so it helps the most variable model.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which model changes most when the rows change?

explain.text: A deep tree has low bias and high variance: exactly what averaging fixes. Stable models, like a stump or OLS, gain almost nothing.
